article.title: Rate limits and monthly usage
article.excerpt: There are two counters, they are not the same number, and only one of them looks like a bill.

p: Every path that submits — API, console, bulk, scheduled — draws on one tenant-level budget. Over the limit returns HTTP 429 with code 42900, and the client is expected to back off.
sections.scope: Figures above are the current published plan limits. Check the pricing page for what applies to your account.

sections.h: There is a second limiter in front
p: An edge limiter also runs, keyed on client IP and set far above any plan tier. It exists to absorb abnormal traffic rather than to shape normal use.
It returns the same HTTP 429 and the same code 42900, so distinguish it by the message text: the edge limiter's message begins with "edge rate limit exceeded".

sections.h: Two counters, and the one that matters
p: The usage endpoint reports both, and they will never be equal.

head: Field
What it counts
rows: How many billable messages you produced — long messages count as more than one, and only provider-accepted ones count
Current plan and its submission ceiling; zero or less means unlimited

sections.h: Why long messages cost more than they look
p: A single logical message can bill as several segments once it crosses the encoding limit, and that limit depends on the alphabet used. Non-GSM characters move the whole message to a wider encoding with a smaller per-segment budget.
The platform does not store message bodies, so segments cannot be recomputed after the fact. The segment count returned with each message is the only record — reconcile from it, not from the text.
